articles.title: Burdens of politicians
articles.content: IT was a humid Sunday afternoon in Islamabad. The small pharmacy was empty with just one man behind the cash counter. A woman approached him, prescription and medicines in hand. She was simply but not shabbily dressed. But she still returned a quarter of the medication once the bill was generated. The man behind the counter explained the bill was around Rs4,000, and she returned about Rs1,000 worth of medication. This took place at a pharmacy in the heart of Islamabad, where real estate sells or rents at eye-watering prices. There was no doctor nearby or a hospital. The woman, chances are, lived close by. It is not a dramatic story or one that really shocks. Tell it to a group of people and they will nod, and, in fact, recount similar stories. Of people’s difficulties. The loans they have taken. How someone got a utility bill higher than their salary. How a colleague had switched from his car to a motorbike. How another had begun shopping for lower-quality food. Conversations such as these abound. And this is before the past week whenpetrol hikes— even those of a daily kind — had begun to hit the headlines. People are now taking bets on when the price of petrol will hit 400 — a far more probable prospect than the cricket team managing a respectable score. That the government realises the impact of the petrol hikes is evident from its announcement torelaunch its subsidy scheme. There is little clarity on how effective the last one had been and how long it lasted, but it’s now back with some tweaks. Ask the government to reduce the petrol levy, and suddenly the big bad IMF enters the conversation; the same IMF which can’t get the government to impose a proper tax ontradersoragriculture incomeor even stop it from giving relief to real estate. Apparently, the petrol levy is the red line. There is little conversation about what inflationary impact this petrol hike will have. And of course, there is little conversation about what inflationary impact this petrol hike will have on food, transport and more — what will happen to the electricity bills, and what this new cycle of inflation will do to already weakened purchasing power. Before the reader rolls her eyes at my audacity to write a piece on the economy, let me clarify that I am about to do no such thing. This is simply going to be a clutch-my-pearls piece on the callousness of the ruling elite. It doesn’t get simpler than that. Long before the Iran war and its impact on the global economy, Pakistan’s human story was already a matter of shame. Our infant mortality rate (46 to 58 deaths per 1,000 births) is higher than the rest of the region and comparable to Afghanistan and Yemen. Nearly 20 per cent of the population has an insufficient caloric intake, and around 40pc of children under five years are malnourished and suffer from stunting — in this, Pakistan is comparable to countries hit by conflict and civil war. The numbers are not recent so as to be linked to the economic mess of the past few years. This is the real story, with facts and figures, along with our own experiences and the anecdotes we all hear of the suffering of the people. But for those ruling us, there is little empathy or awareness of the crisis. This may seem a bit harsh but what else does one say when governments are incapable of curbing even their own lavish personal lifestyles in the face of human misery? The prime minister and his deputy, it seems, spend more time abroad than in the country.Newly born babies recently died in a hospital firein the heart of the capital, petrol is going up faster than pollution, and we already know he isoff to New Yorkon the 20th to tell the world about Pakistan’s efforts in mediation. When one’s home is on fire, shouldn’t saving it be more important? A rhetorical question — for soon we will be subjected to a bunch of ministers and advisers walking on the tarmac and entering a plane. The rest are not far behind. Just recently both the president and thechief minister of Punjabtravelled to Europe on personal visits on private planes. And only widespread criticism forced them both to make public the information that the trips were paid for personally. As if anyone needed any more proof of such disconnect from the lives of ordinary Pakistanis. The president was on a personal visit while the party and the government he heads wasannouncing war on proposals to divide Sindh. If the situation was that dire politically, shouldn’t he have been in Pakistan and in the province? And the Punjab CM — two-and-a-half years later — does not seem to realise that a display of wealth in these times is just poor judgement. Despite the widespread criticism of the aircraft purchased by the Punjab government, it was used for a personal trip. However, this criticism is simply water off a duck’s back. The display of alavish weddingfollowed all of this. This is not to say that politicians should not be allowed private lives; they have every right to it. However, extensive footage and images displaying the grandeur of an event is simply a poor decision. No one expects Pakistan’s ruling elite to behave like their counterparts in the West where ministers carry their own baggage and fly economy. We are far too realistic to expect miracles here but a little discretion can do no harm. And for once, it is not enough to argue that there are powerful people in Pakistan who perhaps enjoy even more perks than politicians but are not spoken about. Indeed, those who take part in electoral exercise and claim to be popular have different burdens than those who simply wield power. And the people in government need to understand this difference.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: To heal a divided family
articles.content: CENTURIES before Charles Darwin theorised our shared human evolution from the fish, multiple traditions linked humanity to a single common fold. The18th BRICS summit in Delhisaw Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as the host leaning on the Sanskrit phrase ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’ — the world is a family — to underpin the spirit of unity, which unfortunately eludes much of mankind. The ancient aphorism is a good but an overstretched reminder of seeing everybody as an equal human being. Some would say that there was perhaps a greater need to find a phrase that frames all Indians as one family before stretching it to include the world. A problem with citing one’s ancient aphorisms at international conferences is that it begins to resemble the Sadda Mian complex. Sadda Mian was a roundly admired elderly Afghan member of Bhopal’s royal family. He would walk along the promenade abutting Bhopal’s vast lake called Bhadbhada, which, he decided, was the largest water body in the world. Another characteristic unique to Sadda Mian was that he fed his domesticated quails with his mouth, tucking the tiny grains of food behind the lower lip. The late thespian Dilip Kumar told me about his invitation to Sadda Mian to visit Bombay where the actor took the genial Pathan to watch the Arabian Sea from the city’s Marine Drive. Sadda Mian, his sherwani unbuttoned and fluttering in the breeze, was so awestruck by the sea’s expanse that he exclaimed gently: “Kya haqeeqat hai Bhadbhade ki!” Sadda Mian’s dumbfounded response translates as: ‘Where does any Bhadbhada hold a chance!’ I looked up a few random traditions from across the lands and seas that don’t seem too different in the spirit of acknowledging the world as a family. But few among them, if any, would be found jumping ecstatically as Newton did watching an apple fall from a tree. There was a time in the early days of Narendra Modi’s rule that the foreign ministry printed and distributed copies of the Bhagavad Gita to foreign dignitaries. In the bargain, the ministry displaced coffee-table books of the Taj, Ajanta caves and Madurai temples. I am not aware of Israel handing out the Torah, or the Vatican presenting the Bible to esteemed visitors, nor does Saudi Arabia or Iran make it a point to offer return gifts of the Holy Quran to visiting dignitaries. Or for that matter, would a privileged guest, returning from China, come home with an officially gifted copy of Mao Zedong Thoughts, or more recently Xi Jinping Thoughts? I bought the Xi book on Amazon. If the world is a family, which it is, talking to the neighbour and sorting out the problem bilaterally is mature. So yes, the world is a family, but what kind of a family? The BRICS summit sought to address some aspects of the troubling question but, by all accounts, it’s going to be a long trudge. Modi said BRICS has come of age — in the sense that the leaders of the UAE and Iran agreeing to meet and not pressing their case too hard to enable asummit statementwas an achievement. One could have accepted the condemnation of theterror attack in Pahalgamand reference to cross-border terrorism as a victory for India. But Pakistan had condemned the attack too. Actually, the BRICS summit in Xiamen in 2017 had gone several steps further when under President Xi’s stewardship it named some extremist outfits allegedly based in Pakistan together with Taliban groups and local security elements for censure. If the world is a family, which it is, talking to the neighbour and sorting out the problem bilaterally is mature. The world brotherhood will applaud. And, yes, the word ‘family’ loses its meaning when someone is seen standing with an aggressor like Israel and visits the country on the eve ofIsrael’s assassination of a revered supreme leaderof a far friendlier country. Also, if the world is a family, let’s stop patronising lynch mobs against fellow humans everywhere. It’s not unlikely that the BRICS summit’s statement slamming Israel’s occupation of Lebanon was a sign of the coming of age. Xi Jinping dominated the show. He said BRICS should become a peacemaker. There needs to be peace within the family. Looking objectively at the idea of global brotherhood with all its warts and wrinkles, the Nehruvian ideal of non-alignment was quite representative of the quest. But Xi, too, has made a forceful intervention to make BRICS more proactive in its quest for global brotherhood. And he stated that BRICS must be a “pioneer in upholding peace and stability”, emphasising that the group needs to actively manage global hotspot issues by addressing both their symptoms and root causes. He clearly outlined a four-point plan for West Asia, focusing on peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adhering to international law, and regional development. It was Xi who reiterated the necessity of pushing for an immediate ceasefire at all the hotspots in West Asia to establish a lasting two-state solution for Palestine to resolve the nub of the crisis. Unlike the Sanskrit phrase cited by Modi, which seems ornamental and ill-fitting given India’s domestic and foreign entanglements with strife, the ancient South African ideal of Ubuntu very crucially was at play when apartheid was dismantled in the country. Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu leaned on the Zulu phrase ‘Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu’. Strikingly similar to the Sanskrit worldview, Ubuntu assured every race and community in the country of equity and equality. The phrase literally means: ‘A person is a person through other persons’ or ‘I am because we are’. The Abrahamic scriptures carry similar messages of a united mankind. The Galatians 3:28 in the Bible says: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This isn’t dissimilar to India’s Maha Upanishad defining narrow-mindedness as calculating ‘this person is a relative, that one is a stranger’. A tricky proposition for Modi to grasp. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Shiny new toys
articles.content: LAST week, an MNA from Islamabad expressed his gratitude to the interior minister for proposing that the capital be given provincial status. The MNA fully backed the minister’s statement, terming this a “long-standing demand of residents of the capital”. This is intriguing for several reasons, not least of which is that in the list of priorities of the capital’s residents one encounters daily, the ‘long-standing demand’ for a new province is not one that features anywhere, let alone prominently. What Islamabad’s residents have categorically demanded, on the other hand, is not being evicted from their land and having their homes bulldozed, access to affordable housing, piped water connections, a functioning solid and liquid waste management system, and a fully integrated public transport network. As far as governance architecture goes, the most tangible demand Islamabad has made for years is having an elected local government — not just a tick-box of procedural democracy, but one that is politically, administratively, and fiscally empowered to deliver its mandate too. Ironically, the MNA referencing the democratic aspirations of his constituency belongs to the ruling party which has delayed LG elections in Islamabad four times over the past four years. Each time, this is done ostensibly to strengthen the structure of a system the residents never actually get to experience. The latest round in this carousel was meant to end in October, when the Election Commission would conclude delimitation and issue an election schedule. However, it is now likely that this will be kicked further down the road as the ruling coalition gears up to introduce a new governance model for Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT). Unlike previous tweaks, this one aims to overhaul the entire system. Provincial status isn’t a priority for Islamabad’s residents. For the uninitiated, the proposed ICT governance model creates a ‘province-like’ status for Islamabad by establishing a 27-member elected legislative assembly, including reserved seats. It provides for a chief executive — likely in the form of a chief minister — and probably a governor. There’s a chief secretary, four secretaries, 26 departments, six specialised authorities. To be fair to this proposal, it has both merits and demerits. Meaningful engagement with the capital’s governance model is long overdue, and this recognition of the need to remedy a fractured system is welcome. There is also much to critique, including the retention of basic powers such as master planning and law and order with the federal government, ambiguities in the executive structure, federal secretaries continuing to govern ICT authorities, and the lack of thought towards reforming fiscal architecture. Since the proposal is still in the works, much may yet be remedied. However, the fatal flaw is not hidden in the details but buried at the foundations. The model creates an effectively bloated structure at the top, while the decay at the grassroots union councils remains unaddressed. It establishes a legislative assembly, without empowering the LGs whose job it is to provide essential service delivery. It may give political leaders a ribbon to cut and a tangible reform package to point towards, but will it make for better results for the residents? Instead of an elaborate new scheme, could more have been achieved by simply extending basic legislative powers to the now-dismembered Metropolitan Corporation of Islamabad? This aspiration to give Islamabad a ‘province-like’ structure has found support in the nationwide frenzy of new provinces, and an already bloated pro- posal may now be pursued beyond its limits. Perhaps the biggest red flag is the confirmation of the earlier perception that this newfound interest in Islamabad’s governance model has something to do with securing an extra NFC share at the centre. This demand is both half-baked and dangerous. The federal government is responsible for Islamabad in the same way that KP is for Peshawar. If the latter is not demanding a separate slice of the NFC to govern its metropolis, then the former’s 42.5 per cent share should also be sufficient. In case it isn’t, it may finally be time to consider meaningful urban fiscal reform that allows cities like Islamabad to raise own-source revenue, particularly through its overpriced real estate. But that will also require political leaders to take on a state-backed property mafia, and we don’t seem ready for that kind of conversation. We’ve heard a lot recently about how the devolution of power is inevitable. Instead of carving up the country into new provinces just to see where it may take us, perhaps we might take the obvious route and try empowering LGs first. Perhaps we might try to work with what we already have instead of chasing shiny new toys. The writer is a governance specialist working on devolution, cities, and climate.
articles.author: Danyal Adam Khan

articles.title: Divide and rule?
articles.content: LEWIS Carroll set a daunting bar in Through the Looking-Glass: one must run to stay in the same place; to get somewhere one must run twice as fast. How far will our one step forward, two steps back gait take us then? Nations once behind us now run twice as fast to perform 21st-century miracles; our rulers still plod after 19th-century mirages. The mirage now being sold to end misrule to entice a nation sick of it is creating many provinces. What they will fix is unclear: low growth or poor services? I dug deep into global research to test this idea but got a blunt rebuke from reform sages: more provinces fix neither; adopt sound policies for growth; devolve, not divide, for better public services. But our rulers avoid such steps. Provinces must ideally focus on policy and large projects; however, ours also control local services. Division will create new patronage layers and fragment policy across small areas; it will keep services poor. Devolving power and purse locally will ensure better services and policy coherence. If research evoked rebuke, global practice evokes alarm. The bottom 15 states on the Fragile States Index average five times more first-tier units than us but have populations only one-fifth of ours. Many created new units in one go. Yet, they are the most fragile and misruled states. Needless division may multiply misrule. Provinces created politically for federal balance and ethnic equity make sense if viable. Punjab comprises over half the federation. The Baloch who form around six per cent of the population have a province; the Seraiki-speaking people, numbering nearly three times as many, do not. A Seraiki unit would improve balance, cutting Punjab’s share to about one-third and being about as big as KP itself. In terms of development, reports rank Seraiki districts far behind Punjab’s dominant ones. But the main minority districts are at par with majority ones in Balochistan and far ahead in Sindh and KP. They would contain nearly 40 million people, big cities like Multan and Bahawalpur, a large agrarian base and be strategically located. A rough review of the net fiscal impact of its NFC share, provincial revenues and Punjab funds lost reveals a small surplus. So, it meets all three tests prima facie. But those based on other minority demands or administrative logic may fail at least two. New provinces require two-thirds votes in parliament and the provincial assembly. A referendum can’t override the Constitution. This makes Sindh’s division hardest given its valid political, fiscal and historical concerns. Bulldozing it via rigged referendums and pliant courts may backfire as, unlike other smaller units, it straddles key trade routes. It rightly said no to the Kalabagh dam and canals project; both remain stalled. The Sindhi-speaking population especially are likely to resist any division. Karachi has huge issues but paradoxical rankings — near-bottom globally among cities; near-top nationally among districts. It exhibits relative individual prosperity and collective adversity. Strong local bodies nationwide will benefit everyone. An Islamabad province would fail at least two tests as a rich region with under 1pc of our population. National capitals globally are usually not made full provinces, more so small ones. Also, a province is just the first step in ensuring equity. So, it is not an ethnicity demanding a province but one that already has one — the Baloch — that is the most aggrieved. Another huge risk is low state capacity for such big changes, evident even in the much simpler Fata merger. New units may emerge on paper but lack capacity, especially in militancy-hit regions where terrorists may exploit the void. Lastly, this set-up’s debatable mandate and hybrid status make such changes contentious. Why do our rulers avoid such systematic analysis and the right policies and sell us only dodgy ideas? Has any set-up ever presented rational policies for public debate, and adopted and implemented them? Only the 18th Amendment and the 1973 Constitution come to mind, both with significant provisos. Nations using top analysts to devise smart policies zoom ahead; we use glib pundits to peddle controversial ideas, and are left trailing behind. Our misrule stems from foundational gaps: lack of legitimate and empowered set-ups. But those blocking them distract us with banal design fixes. Dividing provinces smacks of colonial divide-and-rule ploys. The 26th and 27th Amendments undercut the horizontal balance of power in their favour. A new one may now do so vertically. The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.
articles.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza

articles.title: Rethinking relief
articles.content: THE prime minister’s decision tosubsidisepetrol purchases for motorcycle and small-car owners is understandable amid consumer outcry against high fuel rates. But it is unlikely to offer much relief. The Rs75bn package may sound substantial but is barely a fraction of annual petrol sales. Its reach will be narrower because eligibility depends onconditions such as vehicle and SIM ownership. A monthly subsidy of Rs2,000 for motorcycles and Rs3,000 for small cars may help households, but cannot shield them from sustained global oil price increases. Nor does it assist those who rely on public transport. The question that arises is whether the government is trying to soften the political impact of another fuel price shock. The government must rethink the relief architecture. The BISP National Socio-Economic Registry already has a mechanism to target assistance by household income. Additional support through this system would be more equitable than subsidising a particular fuel purchase. Cash transfers are preferable because recipients can decide whether they need petrol, bus fare, food or another essential. Fuel subsidies make that choice for them and risk encouraging consumption of an imported commodity when foreign exchange pressures are rising. The demand is for acut in the petroleum levyfor broader relief. But the government has little fiscal space for that. Slashing it would create another fiscal hole. Islamabad should, instead, work with the provinces to support public transport users through targeted — and transparent — assistance. The other problem that subsidies cannot solve concernsrising prices of food and other essentials. Fuel price hikes are passed on by transporters and traders to consumers through higher fares and commodity prices; reductions rarely produce equivalent decreases. Provincial and district administrations must monitor this asymmetric pricing more seriously. The global oil market outlook offers little comfort due to the uncertainty caused by the Middle East conflict. Petrol was around $135 a barrel at the end of last week, against the $120-122 benchmark underlying domestic calculations. Every $1 increase in the global benchmark is estimated to add around Rs1.80 per litre to domestic petrol prices. A sustained $10 rise in annual average oil prices could add $1bn-$1.25bn to Pakistan’s import bill, further draining scarce foreign exchange. The pressure could intensify in winter as lower hydropower generation increases reliance on imported fuels and raises electricity costs. The government’s dilemma is clear: higher fuel prices fuel inflation and hurt households, while subsidies put pressure on imports and the fiscal deficit. It has no painless option. Relief must therefore follow need, not vehicle ownership. A poor household using public transport deserves no less consideration than a relatively better-off motorcycle or a small car owner.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Grid disconnect
articles.content: PAKISTAN is about to commit $58bn — or most of this amount — to add new, costlier power capacity it may not need. Nepra’s conditional approval of the Integrated System Plan for 2025-35 deserves closer scrutiny because the regulator’s own members have flagged the problem in their decision. All three recorded dissenting or advisory notes questioning project selection, planning assumptions, and the bypassing of the CCI. That alone should have paused the process. Instead, the plan was approved. Adding 26,045MW under a plan built on the old assumption that demand keeps climbing ignores what is actually happening on the ground. Pakistan already has far more generation capacity than it uses. Consumers are paying for that surplus through some of the region’s highest tariffs, while high power costs have made the country’s exports harder to sell abroad. Rooftop solar has changed the sector’s fundamentals. Households, businesses and farmers are installing their own systems to escape grid electricity they can no longer afford. That shift is already cutting into national grid demand — a trend that will only accelerate as panels and batteries become cheaper. The plan’s 8,120MW net-metering estimate treats this as a fixed number in a market moving too fast. Nepra excluded $900m for battery storage pending a separate study to establish its need. This move might sound reasonable, but approving a plan with no real storage strategy, even as battery imports rise and consumers pair solar with storage to leave the grid further behind, is a mistake. Storage lets the grid soak up extra solar by day and release it at night, easing pressure on costly peak-hour plants. Without it, the solar shift hurts grid finances rather than helping them. As wealthier consumers generate their own power, utilities serve a shrinking base, spreading fixed costs — and higher bills — across fewer people. The outcome may benefit solar adopters but is a financial problem for an already overbuilt grid. ISMO has also reportedly disclaimed responsibility for the accuracy of the data behind the plan. Committing billions of dollars on projections the system operator will not stand behind is recklessness. The government should use the regulator’s own objections to reopen the plan, and build one around the grid that solar, batteries and shifting demand are already creating, not the one planners had imagined a decade ago.
articles.author: Editorial
